hook: That crossed-out price is a trick.
visual_style: Photorealistic cinematic film still, real materials and textures, shallow depth of field, bright retail store light, clean whites with bold red accents
world: A bright American clothing store today, and a wood-panelled 1970s university psychology lab
through_line: a red crossed-out price tag and the number that sticks in your head

cast.Shopper: a man in his 40s, salt-and-pepper hair, navy quilted jacket, tortoiseshell glasses

props.Price tag: a white paper price tag on a string with a bold red diagonal slash across it, no readable text
props.Wheel: a 1970s carnival-style wheel of fortune with red and white wedges and no numbers

places.Lab: a 1970s university psychology lab with wood-panelled walls, a desk and two chairs

cta: Follow for more psychology that saves you money.

captions.hook_line: Stores use this psychology trick on you every single day ⚓
captions.body: In a classic 1974 study, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to land on 10 or 65, then asked an unrelated question; people who saw 65 gave much higher estimates. That first number becomes an anchor. 'Was' prices and opening offers work the same way.
captions.comment_prompt: What's the best 'was' price you've ever fallen for?

youtube_title: The Price Trick Stores Use on You Every Day

sources.claim: Tversky and Kahneman (1974): rigged wheel landing on 10 or 65 anchored estimates of African nations in the UN

blocks.narration: That crossed-out price is a trick. It is called anchoring, and it works on almost everyone. Even when we know it.
blocks.visual: The Price tag swinging on a jacket sleeve in the Store, its bold red slash catch

shots.visual: The Price tag swinging on a jacket sleeve in the Store, its bold red slash catching the light
The Shopper in the Store picking up the jacket, flipping the Price tag over, eyebrows rising
The Shopper smirking knowingly, then still tucking the jacket under his arm
beats: he tucks the jacket under his arm

blocks.narration: In nineteen seventy-four, psychologists spun a rigged wheel of fortune that could only ever stop on ten or sixty-five.
blocks.visual: The Wheel spinning on the desk in the warm 1970s Lab, red and white wedges blurr

shots.visual: The Wheel spinning on the desk in the warm 1970s Lab, red and white wedges blurring
The Wheel slowing and clicking to a stop on a red wedge

blocks.narration: Then they asked people a completely unrelated question. Those who saw sixty-five gave much bigger answers than those who saw ten.
blocks.visual: A volunteer in 1970s clothes sitting across the desk in the Lab, pencil hovering

shots.visual: A volunteer in 1970s clothes sitting across the desk in the Lab, pencil hovering over a blank form
Two volunteers side by side in the Lab, one holding a hand low, the other holding a hand high

blocks.narration: That first number becomes an anchor for everything. Your brain adjusts away from it, but almost never far enough.
blocks.visual: A heavy iron ship anchor dropping onto the Lab desk with a thud, papers flying

shots.visual: A heavy iron ship anchor dropping onto the Lab desk with a thud, papers flying
The Shopper in the Store tilting his head, weighing the jacket in his hands
The Shopper nodding and heading for the register with the jacket

blocks.narration: So a crossed-out two hundred makes ninety-nine feel like a steal. Ask yourself what you would pay without it.
blocks.visual: The Price tag in the Shopper's fingers, the red slash bright under store lights

shots.visual: The Price tag in the Shopper's fingers, the red slash bright under store lights
The Shopper pausing at the register, snipping the Price tag off and looking only at the jacket
